title: 4MAT
definition: 4MAT is an instructional design system by Bernice McCarthy that structures teaching as a four-quadrant learning cycle: Why, What, How, and What If. It moves learners from relevance and motivation through facts and concepts to practical application and transfer, so that one session serves innovative, analytic, common-sense, and dynamic learners alike.

title: 50/72 Rule
definition: The 50/72 Rule is a convention for Git commit messages, popularized by Tim Pope and codified by Chris Beams as the Seven Rules. It asks for an imperative subject line of about 50 characters, a blank line, and a body wrapped at 72 characters that explains why the change was made, not how.

title: A3 Problem Solving
definition: A3 Problem Solving is a problem-solving method from Toyota, set out by John Shook in Managing to Learn, that tells the story of one problem on a single sheet in a fixed sequence. It runs from background and current condition through goal, root cause analysis, and countermeasures to an implementation plan and follow-up: PDCA on one page, rewritten in dialogue with a mentor.

title: ADDIE Model
proponents: Florida State University (origin); Robert Maribe Branch (codification)
definition: The ADDIE Model is a generic process for instructional design, originating at Florida State University and codified by Robert Maribe Branch, named after its five phases: Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, and Evaluation. It leads from clarifying the learning need to delivering and assessing the instruction; modern versions draw it as a cycle in which Evaluation feeds back into every phase.

title: Adobe Spectrum
definition: Adobe Spectrum is Adobe's design system for its desktop, web and mobile applications, in use since 2013 and redesigned as Spectrum 2 from 2023. It ships as React Spectrum, Spectrum Web Components and Spectrum CSS with shared design tokens and the Adobe Clean typeface, and its React implementation builds on the accessible hooks of React Aria.

title: ADR according to Nygard
definition: An Architecture Decision Record according to Michael Nygard is a short, lightweight record of an architecture decision with a fixed structure: Title, Status, Context, Decision, and Consequences. ADRs are stored with the code and never deleted, only superseded, so a team can later understand why past decisions were made.

title: AIDA Model
definition: The AIDA Model — Attention, Interest, Desire, Action — is a persuasion sequence for copywriting and sales, commonly attributed to E. St. Elmo Lewis. It leads the audience through four ordered, narrowing stages, from capturing awareness to a single, clear call to action. It is a heuristic, not a measured model of buyer psychology.

title: Andon
definition: Andon is the signal system of the Toyota Production System, associated with Taiichi Ohno: a board or lamp that shows the status of every station, plus a cord or button that any operator may pull when something is wrong. A pull is first a call for help; the line stops only at the next fixed position if nobody resolves the problem in time. The authority to signal, not the hardware, is the design, and software borrows it for red builds and halted rollouts.

title: Ant Design
definition: Ant Design is the enterprise design language and React component library (antd) from Ant Group, the Alibaba affiliate behind Alipay, released publicly in 2015. Built for data-heavy admin and back-office interfaces, it offers components such as Form, Table and ConfigProvider, and a theme system of seed, map and alias tokens.

title: Apple Human Interface Guidelines
definition: The Apple Human Interface Guidelines are Apple's design guidance for iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS, tvOS and visionOS. They cover hit regions of at least 44 by 44 points as a general rule and 60 by 60 in visionOS, SF Pro and SF Symbols, Dynamic Type, navigation patterns, system colours and accessibility, and since 2025 the Liquid Glass material.

title: arc42 Architecture Documentation
definition: arc42 is a template for documenting software architecture, created by Gernot Starke and Peter Hruschka. It organises an architecture into twelve standardised sections — from goals, constraints, and context through building blocks, runtime, and deployment to decisions, quality, and risks — so teams document consistently and completely.

title: Arrange-Act-Assert (AAA)
definition: Arrange-Act-Assert is a structure for the body of a single unit test, named by Bill Wake: set up the object under test, perform exactly one action on it, then make claims about the result. It matches the first three phases of Gerard Meszaros' Four-Phase Test and leaves teardown implicit; a second action means a second test.

title: ATAM
definition: ATAM, the Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method by Rick Kazman, Mark Klein and Paul Clements of the SEI at Carnegie Mellon University, evaluates a software architecture against its quality goals. A utility tree breaks those goals into prioritized quality attribute scenarios, and a nine-step process analyzes the architectural approaches against them. The result names sensitivity points, tradeoff points where one decision affects several quality attributes in conflicting ways, and risks and non-risks.

title: Atlassian Design System
definition: The Atlassian Design System is the design system behind Jira, Confluence and Trello, first published as the Atlassian Design Guidelines (ADG) in 2013. It provides the Atlaskit React components, design tokens for colour, elevation, spacing and typography such as color.text.subtle and space.100, and the Atlassian Sans typeface.

title: Atomic Design
definition: Atomic Design is Brad Frost's methodology for building design systems from five levels: atoms, molecules, organisms, templates and pages. Small elements combine into larger components and finally into pages with real content, which gives component libraries a shared structure.

title: Bauhaus
definition: Bauhaus was the German school of design founded by Walter Gropius in Weimar in 1919 and closed in Berlin in 1933. As a design instruction, the name evokes the style later drawn from it: form follows function, basic geometric shapes such as circle, square and triangle, primary colours, geometric sans-serif type and the unity of art, craft and industry.

title: BDD (Behavior-Driven Development)
definition: Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) is Dan North's practice, introduced in 2006, of specifying system behavior through concrete examples that double as executable tests. Scenarios follow the Given-When-Then format and are written in Gherkin syntax, in a ubiquitous language that developers, testers and business representatives work out together in Three Amigos sessions. The scenarios serve as executable acceptance criteria and as living documentation that stays current with the system.

title: BEM Methodology
definition: BEM (Block Element Modifier) is a naming methodology for CSS and SCSS from the Yandex development team. Each class name follows the blockelement--modifier structure: a block is a standalone component, an element is a part of a block with no meaning on its own, and a modifier is a flag that changes appearance or behavior. Flat selectors and explicit names avoid specificity wars and naming conflicts in large codebases.

title: Bento Grid
definition: A bento grid is a layout of rounded tiles in different sizes on one grid, each tile holding one feature, figure or image. Size carries the hierarchy, usually with one large hero tile and smaller tiles around it; the layout became popular through Apple's product presentations.

title: Big Five (OCEAN) Personality Traits
definition: The Big Five, or Five-Factor Model, is a trait model of personality that goes back to Lewis R. Goldberg and to Paul T. Costa and Robert R. McCrae. It describes people along five continuous dimensions — Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism (OCEAN) — instead of sorting them into types. The model is descriptive and predictive, not causal.

title: BlinkWithoutDelay
definition: BlinkWithoutDelay is the built-in Arduino example sketch, created by David A. Mellis, that blinks an LED by comparing millis() timestamps instead of calling delay(). It stands for non-blocking timing in a superloop: each task keeps its own timestamp and interval, checks the elapsed time with overflow-safe subtraction on every pass, and nothing ever waits.

title: Bloom’s Taxonomy
definition: Bloom's Taxonomy is a classification of learning objectives by cognitive level, created by Benjamin Bloom et al. in 1956 and revised by Lorin Anderson and David Krathwohl in 2001. The revised version orders six levels from lower to higher order, Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate and Create, each with measurable action verbs. It turns vague aims into testable objectives and pushes assessment above mere recall.

title: BLUF (Bottom Line Up Front)
proponents: adopted broadly in business and government
definition: BLUF — Bottom Line Up Front — is a communication structure from US military practice: state the conclusion, decision, or key request in the very first sentence, then give the supporting detail. The reader gets the essential takeaway immediately instead of reading to the end to find it.

title: Bootstrap 5
definition: Bootstrap 5 is the fifth major version of the front-end toolkit that Mark Otto and Jacob Thornton released at Twitter in 2011. It provides a 12-column flexbox grid with six breakpoints, a utility API, Sass and CSS custom properties, colour modes since 5.3 and ready-made components with class names such as form-control and btn-primary, and it no longer depends on jQuery.

title: Boy Scout Rule
definition: The Boy Scout Rule is Robert C. Martin's transfer to code of the Boy Scouts' rule to leave the campground cleaner than you found it: check a module in cleaner than you checked it out. The cleanup stays small and limited to code the current task already touches, such as renaming an unclear variable or deleting dead code. It counters the slow decay of a codebase and assumes a green test suite.

title: Bulkhead Pattern
definition: The Bulkhead pattern is a stability pattern from Michael T. Nygard's Release It! that partitions a finite resource, such as threads, connections or instances, so that each dependency, tenant or workload gets its own slice. Named after the sectioned partitions of a ship's hull, it lets one slow or failing consumer exhaust only its own slice while the rest keep working. It is built as a thread-pool or semaphore bulkhead and combined with timeouts and circuit breakers.

title: C4-Diagrams
definition: The C4 model is Simon Brown's approach to software architecture diagrams at four levels of abstraction: Context, Container, Component, and Code. Readers zoom from a system in its environment down to its classes, with a simple boxes-and-arrows notation and different diagrams for different stakeholders.

title: CAP Theorem
definition: The CAP theorem, conjectured by Eric Brewer in 2000 and formally proved by Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch in 2002, states that a distributed system cannot guarantee both consistency and availability during a network partition. Because real networks partition, the actual design choice is CP or AP behavior while partitioned. Daniel Abadi's PACELC extension of 2012 adds the trade-off between latency and consistency when no partition occurs.

title: Carbon Design System
definition: The Carbon Design System is IBM's open-source design system, developed in public since 2015 as the digital form of the IBM Design Language. It combines IBM Plex type with productive and expressive type sets, the 16-column 2x Grid, four themes from White to Gray 100, design tokens such as layer-01, and components in @carbon/react and @carbon/web-components.

title: Chain of Thought (CoT)
proponents: "Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models"
definition: Chain of Thought (CoT) is a prompting technique for large language models that asks the model to reason step by step before stating a final answer. Making the intermediate steps explicit improves accuracy on multi-step arithmetic, logic, and reasoning tasks compared with answering directly.

title: Chesterton’s Fence
definition: Chesterton's Fence is a principle based on G.K. Chesterton's parable in The Thing (1929): do not clear away a fence across a road until you know why it was put up. It moves the burden of proof onto whoever wants to remove something and treats an unexplained artifact as evidence of a past failure. In software it asks for a timeboxed investigation of legacy code before deletion, after which a reversible removal is allowed.

title: Circuit Breaker
definition: The Circuit Breaker is a stability pattern introduced by Michael Nygard in Release It! and popularized further by Martin Fowler. It guards calls to a protected resource and trips once failures cross a threshold, so further calls fail fast instead of blocking; after a reset timeout it lets a trial call through to test recovery. This prevents resource exhaustion and cascading failure.

title: Clean Architecture
definition: Clean Architecture, formulated by Robert C. Martin, organises code into concentric layers whose dependencies point only inward toward the domain. Business rules sit at the centre, independent of frameworks, UI, and databases at the outer edges. The Dependency Rule keeps the core testable and insulated from external change.

title: Cockburn Use Cases
definition: Cockburn Use Cases are Alistair Cockburn's prose-based format for describing system behavior from an actor's perspective, set out in Writing Effective Use Cases (2001). The fully dressed template covers primary actor, stakeholders and interests, preconditions, trigger, a numbered main success scenario, extensions and postconditions. Goal levels (summary, user goal, subfunction), an explicit scope and an actor-goal list keep each use case at the right granularity, with the user goal as the sweet spot.

title: Code Smells
definition: Code smells are surface indications in code that usually point to a deeper design problem; Kent Beck coined the term, and Martin Fowler's Refactoring (1999, 2nd ed. 2018) made it standard vocabulary. Each smell, such as Long Method, Shotgun Surgery or Feature Envy, is a heuristic that shows where to look and is paired with a refactoring that typically resolves it. Robert C. Martin's Clean Code (2008) extends the catalogue with about 65 heuristics.

title: Cohesion Criteria
definition: The Cohesion Criteria are a seven-level scale by Larry Constantine and Edward Yourdon for rating how strongly the elements of a module belong together. It runs from coincidental cohesion, the worst, through logical, temporal, procedural, communicational, and sequential cohesion to functional cohesion, the ideal, and lets you judge module quality by concrete criteria instead of gut feeling.

title: CQS (Command-Query Separation)
tags: asking a question should not change the answer
definition: Command-Query Separation (CQS) is Bertrand Meyer's design rule from Object-Oriented Software Construction (1988): every method is either a command, which changes state and returns nothing, or a query, which returns a value and changes no observable state, never both. Asking a question then does not change the answer, so queries are safe to repeat and to call from contracts and assertions. It is a per-method rule, distinct from the architectural pattern CQRS.

title: Connextra User Story Format
tags: As a I want so that
definition: The Connextra user story format is the three-part user story template devised at Connextra in London and popularised by Mike Cohn: “As a …, I want …, so that …”. Its three slots name who, what, and why. It fixes the shape of the sentence, not the quality of the story, and the card stands for a conversation rather than the requirement itself.

title: Consent vs. Consensus
definition: Consent vs. Consensus is the distinction between two group decision rules; consent was formalized in Gerard Endenburg's sociocracy and Brian Robertson's Holacracy. Consensus needs everyone to actively agree, consent only the absence of a paramount, reasoned objection — good enough for now, safe enough to try. Valid objections are integrated into an amended proposal instead of acting as a veto.

title: Control Chart (Shewhart)
definition: The Shewhart Control Chart is a time-series diagram developed by Walter A. Shewhart at Bell Labs and Western Electric, and the central tool of Statistical Process Control. It plots a measured value around a centerline with upper and lower control limits, typically at ±3σ, to separate the common-cause variation of a stable process from assignable special causes.

title: Conventional Commits
definition: Conventional Commits is a specification for adding human- and machine-readable meaning to commit messages, with Benjamin E. Coe, James J. Womack and Steve Mao as key proponents. Each message follows a schema of type, optional scope and description, with types such as feat, fix, docs or refactor, and an exclamation mark or BREAKING CHANGE footer for breaking changes. The types determine the semantic version bump and tell teammates and other stakeholders what kind of change landed.

title: Conway’s Law
definition: Conway's Law is Melvin E. Conway's observation, published in Datamation in 1968, that any organization that designs a system will produce a design whose structure copies the organization's communication structure. Interfaces in the software appear where teams must coordinate, so org design and system design are two sides of the same decision. The Inverse Conway Maneuver applies the law deliberately by shaping teams to match the desired architecture.

title: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation)
definition: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) is a pattern, coined by Greg Young, that lifts Bertrand Meyer's Command Query Separation from methods to models: writes and reads go through separate models, each optimized for its purpose. Domain events propagate changes from the write side to read-side projections, accepting eventual consistency so that both sides can scale independently. Event sourcing complements CQRS but is not required.

title: CRC-Cards
definition: CRC Cards — Class-Responsibility-Collaboration Cards — are a low-tech object-oriented design technique by Ward Cunningham and Kent Beck that puts one class on each index card, with its responsibilities on the left and its collaborators on the right. Teams walk through scenarios by role-playing the cards and so discover and refine classes before writing code.

title: Crisis and Emergency Risk Communication (CERC)
proponents: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
definition: Crisis and Emergency Risk Communication (CERC) is a framework for communicating before the facts are in, set out as an integrative model by Barbara Reynolds and Matthew W. Seeger and taught by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Its six principles are Be First, Be Right, Be Credible, Express Empathy, Promote Action and Show Respect. Messages follow the crisis lifecycle from preparation through initial reaction, maintenance and resolution to evaluation.

title: CUPID Properties
definition: CUPID is Dan North's set of five properties of joyful code: Composable, Unix philosophy, Predictable, Idiomatic and Domain-based. Unlike principles, which code either follows or breaks, properties are qualities that code has more or less of and that you move toward. North positions the set against SOLID, arguing that pleasant code comes from overlapping qualities that reinforce each other rather than from class-level rules.

title: Curse of Knowledge
definition: The Curse of Knowledge is a cognitive bias, named by Colin Camerer, George Loewenstein and Martin Weber in 1989 and popularized by Chip Heath and Dan Heath: once you know something, you can hardly reconstruct what it was like not to know it. Experts therefore overestimate shared context, leave jargon undefined and skip steps. The antidote is to make hidden assumptions explicit, define terms and test the text against a representative reader.

title: Cynefin Framework
definition: Cynefin, created by Dave Snowden, is a sense-making framework that sorts situations into five domains — Clear, Complicated, Complex, Chaotic, and Confused — each with a different cause-and-effect relationship. It helps choose the right response, from applying best practice in ordered domains to probing and experimenting in the complex one.

title: Dale Carnegie Principles
tags: How to Win Friends and Influence People
definition: The Dale Carnegie Principles are the rules for dealing with people from Dale Carnegie's How to Win Friends and Influence People (1936). They include not criticising, condemning or complaining, giving honest and sincere appreciation, arguing from the other person's interest, pointing out mistakes indirectly so the other person can save face, and asking questions instead of giving orders. They govern how a correction is delivered, not whether it is made.

title: Decisional Balance Sheet
definition: The Decisional Balance Sheet is a decision aid formalized by Irving Janis and Leon Mann that lists, for each alternative, gains and losses for self and for significant others, self-approval or disapproval, and approval or disapproval from others. Its everyday ancestor is Benjamin Franklin's two-column pros-and-cons list. Its main purpose is to surface unspoken concerns and resolve ambivalence, not to mechanise the choice.

title: Deep Modules
definition: Deep Modules is John Ousterhout's design principle from A Philosophy of Software Design: a module should offer a lot of functionality behind a small, stable interface. Because every interface element is a cost callers must pay, deep modules hide design decisions likely to change, while shallow modules, whose interface is nearly as complex as their implementation, push complexity onto callers.

title: Defense in Depth
definition: Defense in Depth is a security strategy, adapted from military doctrine and set out for information assurance in an NSA paper, that protects a system with several layers of controls across people, technology, and operations. The layers count only if they are independent and diverse and each assumes the one before it has already been breached; detection and recovery are layers too.

title: Defensive Programming according to McConnell
definition: Defensive Programming according to McConnell is the coding practice set out in chapter 8 of Steve McConnell's Code Complete (2nd edition, 2004): protect a program from invalid input so that bad data never yields a quiet wrong result. A barricade divides the code; public interfaces outside it validate input and handle errors, while code inside assumes clean data and uses assertions for conditions that must never occur. Each system also chooses between robustness and correctness.

title: Definition of Done
definition: The Definition of Done is a formal, team-wide checklist of quality criteria that every increment must satisfy before it counts as done, as described by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland in The Scrum Guide (2020). Typical gates are code reviewed, tests passing, documentation updated and no known defects. It makes the meaning of done transparent to all stakeholders, work that misses it returns to the Product Backlog, and the team tightens it as it matures.

title: Design by Contract
definition: Design by Contract is a design approach by Bertrand Meyer, coined for the Eiffel language, that treats each routine as a contract between caller and implementation. Preconditions state the caller's obligations, postconditions the routine's guarantees, and class invariants the conditions every instance keeps; a violated clause shows which side holds the bug.

title: Design Tokens (W3C DTCG)
definition: Design tokens in the W3C DTCG format store design decisions such as colours, spacing and type as platform-neutral JSON, with $value and $type per token and aliases in braces. The Design Tokens Community Group published its first stable version, 2025.10; tools convert the tokens into CSS, iOS and Android code.

title: Devil’s Advocate
proponents: Roman Catholic Church (advocatus diaboli / Promotor Fidei)
definition: Devil's Advocate is the practice of deliberately arguing against a proposal, even without holding that view, to stress-test it before a decision. It derives from the Promotor Fidei role in the Catholic Church's canonization process, formalized in 1587, and was later adopted in law, philosophy, business strategy and red teaming. Done well, it presents the strongest opposing argument, surfaces hidden assumptions and identifies risks early.

title: Diátaxis Framework
definition: Diátaxis is Daniele Procida's framework for organizing technical documentation into four types: tutorials, how-to guides, reference, and explanation. The types follow two dimensions, practical versus theoretical and learning versus working, so each serves a distinct user need and has its own quality criteria.

title: Dieter Rams' 10 Principles of Good Design
definition: Dieter Rams' ten principles of good design say that good design is innovative, useful, aesthetic, understandable, unobtrusive, honest, long-lasting, thorough down to the last detail, environmentally friendly, and as little design as possible. The Braun designer summed them up as "less, but better": remove the unnecessary rather than imitate a minimal look.

title: DISC Model (Marston)
advisory: Classified as pseudoscience with no demonstrated predictive validity — use for reflection and dialogue, not selection (see Criticism)
definition: The DISC Model is a theory of behavioural styles that William Moulton Marston proposed in 1928. In its modern form it sorts behaviour into four quadrants — Dominance, Influence, Steadiness, and Conscientiousness — which arise from two axes: how a person perceives the environment and how much control they feel within it. It describes communication style, not ability, and its scientific validity has not been demonstrated.

title: DMADV
definition: DMADV — Define, Measure, Analyze, Design, Verify — is the Six Sigma roadmap for designing a new product, service, or process, also known as Design for Six Sigma (DFSS). It turns the Voice of the Customer into measurable CTQs, compares design concepts, predicts each CTQ’s capability from models, and verifies that prediction on pilot output. It builds quality in at the design stage instead of improving an existing process, as DMAIC does.

title: DMAIC
definition: DMAIC — Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control — is the Six Sigma improvement cycle for existing processes, standardised in ISO 13053-1:2011. Its five phases run in fixed order behind formal tollgates: define the problem, establish a measured baseline, validate root causes against the data, pilot solutions, and hold the gain with a control plan. Its distinguishing trait is that sustaining the improvement is a phase of its own.

title: Docs-as-Code according to Ralf D. Müller
definition: Docs-as-Code according to Ralf D. Müller, the creator of docToolchain, treats documentation like code: written in plain-text formats such as AsciiDoc, kept in Git alongside the code, reviewed through pull requests and built by automated toolchains. Diagrams are written as code too, for example in PlantUML, and one source generates multiple output formats such as HTML and PDF. This keeps the documentation synchronized with the code it describes.

title: Domain-Driven Design according to Evans
definition: Domain-Driven Design, introduced by Eric Evans, tackles complex software by centring the design on the business domain. A shared Ubiquitous Language unites developers and domain experts, Bounded Contexts delimit models, and tactical patterns — entities, value objects, aggregates, repositories — express the domain directly in code.

title: Domain Storytelling according to Hofer and Schwentner
definition: Domain Storytelling, as described by Stefan Hofer and Henning Schwentner, is a collaborative modeling method in which domain experts tell concrete stories about their work while a moderator draws them in a pictographic language. Actors and work objects appear as icons, activities as arrows labelled with domain verbs, and sequence numbers turn the picture into readable sentences. Each diagram shows one concrete case, and the stories help find bounded contexts and a shared domain language.

title: Double Diamond
definition: The Double Diamond is the UK Design Council's design process model, first published in 2005, with four phases: Discover, Define, Develop and Deliver. Each of its two diamonds is a divergent-convergent cycle; the first explores and frames the problem, the second explores and ships the solution. Its summary is to design the right thing, then design the thing right, and the 2019 Framework for Innovation made iteration between the phases explicit.

title: Dreyfus Model of Skill Acquisition
definition: The Dreyfus Model of Skill Acquisition is a five-stage model of how adults acquire skill, published by Stuart E. and Hubert L. Dreyfus in 1980. Learners move from Novice through Advanced Beginner, Competent, and Proficient to Expert, shifting from rigid, context-free rule-following to fluid, intuitive pattern recognition. Each stage needs a different kind of guidance: novices want rules, experts want holistic context.

title: DRY (Don’t Repeat Yourself)
definition: DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) is the principle from Andy Hunt and Dave Thomas's The Pragmatic Programmer (1999) that every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation within a system. It targets duplicated knowledge and intent, such as a business rule or a schema, not code that merely looks alike. Other artifacts are derived from one source of truth, and abstraction waits for the Rule of Three, because the wrong abstraction costs more than duplication.

title: EARS-Requirements
definition: EARS — the Easy Approach to Requirements Syntax — is a set of sentence templates for writing requirements, with Alistair Mavin (Rolls-Royce) as its key proponent. It offers five patterns: ubiquitous (“The system shall …”), event-driven (WHEN), unwanted behaviour (IF … THEN), state-driven (WHILE), and optional feature (WHERE). The consistent structure makes each requirement clear and verifiable.

title: Effective Go
definition: Effective Go is the Go Authors’ guide to writing idiomatic Go, written for the language’s release in 2009. It covers gofmt formatting, package names, defer, goroutines and channels (“share memory by communicating”), implicitly satisfied interfaces, errors as values, and composition through embedding. It remains a guide to the core language but is not actively updated and does not cover modules or generics.

title: Effective Java
definition: Effective Java is Joshua Bloch's book of Java best practices, published by Addison-Wesley and organized as a catalog of about 90 short, self-contained Items, each a concrete rule with rationale and trade-offs. The Items cover object creation, the equals and hashCode contracts, minimizing mutability, composition over inheritance, generics with the PECS rule, enums, lambdas and streams, exceptions and concurrency. The 3rd edition of December 2017 is the current one.

title: Effective Python
definition: Effective Python is Brett Slatkin's book of Python best practices, published by Addison-Wesley and organized as a catalog of short, self-contained Items, each a concrete rule with rationale and trade-offs. The Items cover Pythonic style, comprehensions and generators, function arguments, class design with properties, metaclasses, concurrency under the GIL, robustness and testing. The current 3rd edition of 20 November 2024 expands the 2nd edition's 90 Items to 125.

title: 8-Point Grid
definition: The 8-point grid is a spacing system for user interfaces in which all margins, paddings and component sizes are multiples of eight, with four as a half-step for type and icons. Popularised by Material Design's 8dp baseline grid and Bryn Jackson's guide, it keeps spacing consistent across screens.

title: Eisenhower Matrix
advisory: Activates an urgency-first framing its own field cautions against (see Criticism)
definition: The Eisenhower Matrix is a prioritization tool that plots every task on two independent axes, urgency and importance. Dwight D. Eisenhower is credited with popularizing the distinction in a 1954 speech, and Stephen Covey turned it into the four-quadrant Time Management Matrix in The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (1989). The quadrants map to four actions, do, schedule, delegate and delete, and Covey calls important but not urgent work the heart of effective personal management.

title: The Elements of Typographic Style (Bringhurst)
definition: The Elements of Typographic Style is Robert Bringhurst's 1992 reference work on book typography, now in version 4.0. As an instruction it brings a comfortable measure, careful leading, old-style figures in running text, small caps for abbreviations, indented paragraphs and hanging punctuation.

title: Enterprise Integration Patterns (Hohpe/Woolf)
definition: Enterprise Integration Patterns is the pattern language for messaging solutions by Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf, published by Addison-Wesley in 2003 and maintained as an online catalog of 65 patterns. It first compares four integration styles, File Transfer, Shared Database, Remote Procedure Invocation and Messaging, then sorts the patterns into six categories along a message's journey. Pipes and filters is the base metaphor, so patterns such as Message Channel, Message Router and Message Translator compose.

title: Event-Driven Architecture
definition: Event-Driven Architecture is an architectural style in which components communicate by emitting and reacting to events instead of calling each other directly, with Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf (2003) and Martin Fowler (2017) as key proponents. Producers publish events without knowing their consumers, and message queues decouple both sides in time. The price is at-least-once delivery, which requires idempotent consumers, and eventual consistency; workflows run by choreography or orchestration.

title: Event Storming according to Alberto Brandolini
definition: Event Storming is Alberto Brandolini's collaborative workshop format, first run in 2012, for modeling a business domain as past-tense domain events placed on a timeline along a wide wall. A fixed colour notation adds commands, aggregates, policies, read models, external systems and hotspots, and the workshop works at three levels: Big Picture, Process Modeling and Design Level. Pivotal events mark candidate bounded context boundaries, which makes it a common on-ramp to Domain-Driven Design.

title: Every Layout
definition: Every Layout is a book and website by Heydon Pickering and Andy Bell that builds responsive CSS layouts from small primitives such as Stack, Cluster, Sidebar, Switcher and Grid. The primitives adapt to their content and container, so most layouts need no media queries and no magic numbers.

title: Fagan Inspection
definition: Fagan Inspection is the formal review process for software artifacts that Michael Fagan described in the IBM Systems Journal in 1976. A moderator, the author, inspectors and a recorder take defined roles and move through six phases, Planning, Overview, Preparation, Inspection Meeting, Rework and Follow-up, each with entry and exit criteria. Defects are classified by type and severity, and the collected metrics improve both the product and the inspection process.

title: Fallacies of Distributed Computing
definition: The Fallacies of Distributed Computing are eight false assumptions about networks; L. Peter Deutsch named the first seven at Sun Microsystems around 1994, and James Gosling added the eighth. They are: the network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite, the network is secure, topology doesn't change, there is one administrator, transport cost is zero, and the network is homogeneous. Used as an audit checklist, they expose designs that would fail under real network conditions.

title: Fermi Estimation
definition: Fermi Estimation is a technique, associated with Enrico Fermi, for estimating an unknown quantity to the right order of magnitude by breaking it into a chain of smaller quantities that can each be guessed. Each sub-quantity is bracketed between plausible bounds, and independent over- and under-estimates tend to cancel, so the result often lands within a factor of 2-3 of the true value. It serves to size systems and sanity-check claims before investing in precision.

title: Feynman Technique
definition: The Feynman Technique is a learning method named after the physicist Richard Feynman that tests understanding by explaining a concept in simple language, as if to a beginner. Its four steps are to choose a concept, teach it in plain terms, find the gaps where the explanation fails and return to the source material, then simplify with analogies and repeat until the explanation is clear and free of jargon.

title: Fichtean Curve
definition: The Fichtean Curve is a crisis-driven story structure, named after Johann Gottlieb Fichte and popularised by John Gardner and Janet Burroway, that opens in medias res and drives the plot through a series of escalating crises. Each crisis forces a consequential choice that leads to the next, until a climax resolves the central conflict, followed by a brief falling action. Backstory enters only as needed, which keeps short stories and genre fiction fast.

title: Finite State Machine
definition: A finite state machine is a model of behaviour built from a finite, named set of states and the events that trigger transitions between them; George H. Mealy (1955) and Edward F. Moore (1956) defined its two classic output models. A transition table lists every combination of state and event, so each cell becomes an explicit decision. David Harel’s statecharts add hierarchy and concurrency and underlie UML state machines.

title: First Principles Thinking
definition: First Principles Thinking is a reasoning method, rooted in Aristotle and sharpened by René Descartes' methodical doubt, that breaks a problem down to basic truths which cannot be deduced from anything more fundamental and then reasons upward from them. It contrasts with reasoning by analogy: each inherited constraint is tested as law of nature or mere convention, and the irreducible elements are recombined into a new solution. Being costly, it suits high-stakes or stuck problems.

title: Five Whys (Ohno)
definition: Five Whys is a root cause analysis technique from the Toyota Production System, associated with Sakichi Toyoda and Taiichi Ohno, in which a team asks why about five times to get from a symptom to an actionable root cause. Each answer feeds the next question, and the chain ends in a countermeasure. Critics such as Alan J. Card and John Allspaw argue that a single linear chain cannot capture the interacting factors behind incidents in complex systems.

title: Fluent 2 Design System
definition: Fluent 2 is Microsoft's design system for Microsoft 365, Teams and Windows, released in 2023 as the successor of the Fluent Design System of 2017. It defines global and alias design tokens, a type ramp in Segoe UI and platform typefaces, and components for web, Windows, iOS and Android, on the web through Fluent UI React v9.

title: FMEA
definition: FMEA, Failure Mode and Effects Analysis, is a bottom-up, forward-looking risk method, first described in 1949 in the US military document MIL-P-1629, that asks for each component or process step how it can fail. For every failure mode it records effect, cause and controls and rates Severity, Occurrence and Detection. Classic FMEA ranks risks by the Risk Priority Number, while the AIAG and VDA handbook of 2019 replaced it with Action Priority and a seven-step process.

title: 4+1 View Model according to Kruchten
definition: The 4+1 View Model is Philippe Kruchten’s scheme for describing software architecture, published in IEEE Software in 1995. It describes a system through four views — logical, development, process, and physical — each answering the question of a named audience, plus a small set of key scenarios. The scenarios help discover architectural elements and then cross-check the four views for consistency.

title: Four-Sides Model (Schulz von Thun)
definition: The Four-Sides Model is Friedemann Schulz von Thun's model of communication, published in 1981, which holds that every message carries four sides at once: factual information, self-revelation, relationship and appeal. The receiver decodes them with four matching ears, and misunderstanding arises when the sender stresses one side while the receiver hears another. The model builds on Karl Bühler's Organon model and Paul Watzlawick's content and relationship axiom.

title: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (PEAA)
definition: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (PEAA) is Martin Fowler’s 2002 catalog of patterns for building enterprise applications. It groups them into domain logic, data source, object-relational, web presentation, distribution, offline concurrency, session state, and base patterns — among them Transaction Script, Domain Model, Active Record, Data Mapper, Unit of Work, and Repository. Many of these patterns are now implemented by common frameworks.

title: Freytag’s Pyramid
definition: Freytag’s Pyramid is a model of dramatic structure from Gustav Freytag’s “Die Technik des Dramas” (1863), derived from five-act stage tragedy. It divides a story into exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, and dénouement: tension builds to a turning point and then releases into a final equilibrium — restoration in comedy, collapse in tragedy.

title: Genchi Genbutsu
definition: Genchi Genbutsu (現地現物, “the actual place, the actual thing”) is the Toyota principle of going to see for yourself, one of the five principles of the Toyota Way 2001. The person who decides must observe the work where it happens and look at the thing itself, not at reports about it. It is the observation step that cause-hunting methods such as Five Whys depend on.

title: Gestalt Principles
definition: The Gestalt principles describe how people group what they see: elements that are close, similar, enclosed, connected or moving together are perceived as one unit, and figures separate from their ground. Formulated by Max Wertheimer in 1923, they explain why a layout reads as grouped or scattered.

title: Gherkin
definition: Gherkin is the structured, plain-language syntax used by Behaviour-Driven Development tools such as Cucumber to write executable specifications. Scenarios follow a Given/When/Then form — context, action, outcome — so the same text serves as readable acceptance criteria for stakeholders and as automated tests.

title: GitHub Flow
definition: GitHub Flow is a lightweight, branch-based Git workflow described by Scott Chacon in 2011, in which main is always deployable. Every change gets a short-lived branch from main, and a Pull Request serves for review, discussion and CI validation before the merge. In Chacon's original formulation each merge is deployed immediately, while GitHub's current official description ends at the merge without a deployment step.

title: Glassmorphism
definition: Glassmorphism is a UI style of translucent, frosted-glass panels that blur the colourful background behind them, float on separate layers and carry a subtle light border. Michał Malewicz named it in 2020; in CSS it rests on semi-transparent fills and backdrop-filter blur.

title: GoF-Abstract Factory Pattern
definition: The Abstract Factory pattern, also known as Kit, is a creational GoF design pattern by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides that provides an interface for creating families of related or dependent objects without specifying their concrete classes. A system configured with one factory gets products from one family only, which keeps it independent of how products are created and enforces that related products are used together.

title: GoF-Adapter Pattern
definition: The Adapter pattern, also known as Wrapper, is a structural GoF design pattern by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides that converts the interface of a class into another interface clients expect. The adapter sits between client and existing class and translates calls, so a class whose interface does not match can be reused, for example to map a legacy API onto a new interface without changing existing code.

title: GoF-Bridge Pattern
definition: The Bridge pattern is a structural GoF design pattern by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides that decouples an abstraction from its implementation so that the two can vary independently. Abstraction and implementation sit in separate class hierarchies, each extensible by subclassing, which avoids a permanent binding between them and keeps changes in the implementation from affecting clients.

title: GoF-Builder Pattern
definition: The Builder pattern is a creational GoF design pattern by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides that separates the construction of a complex object from its representation, so that the same construction process can create different representations. The algorithm that assembles the object stays independent of its parts and how they are put together, which suits step-by-step construction such as a fluent API for a query object.

title: GoF-Chain of Responsibility Pattern
definition: The Chain of Responsibility pattern is a behavioral GoF design pattern by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides that avoids coupling the sender of a request to its receiver by giving more than one object a chance to handle it. The receiving objects form a chain, and each handler either processes the request or passes it to the next. The set of handlers can be specified dynamically, as in a middleware pipeline.

title: GoF-Command Pattern
definition: The Command pattern is a behavioral GoF design pattern by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides that encapsulates a request as an object. Because each action becomes an object, clients can be parameterized with different requests, and requests can be queued, logged or scheduled. Commands also support undoable operations, which makes the pattern a common basis for undo and redo systems.

title: GoF-Composite Pattern
definition: The Composite pattern is a structural GoF design pattern by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides that composes objects into tree structures to represent part-whole hierarchies. Individual objects and compositions share one interface, so clients treat them uniformly and can ignore the difference between a single object and a group, as when files and folders in a file system are handled the same way.

title: GoF-Decorator Pattern
definition: The Decorator pattern, also known as Wrapper, is a structural GoF design pattern by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides that attaches additional responsibilities to an object dynamically. Decorators wrap the object and add behavior transparently, which offers a flexible alternative to subclassing when extension by inheritance is impractical, for example to add formatting, timestamps and filtering to a logger.

title: GoF Design Patterns
definition: The GoF Design Patterns are the 23 object-oriented design patterns that Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson, and John Vlissides — the “Gang of Four” — catalogued in “Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software” (1994). They fall into creational, structural, and behavioral patterns and give developers a shared vocabulary for recurring design problems and proven solutions. Underlying principles include composition over inheritance and programming to an interface.

title: GoF-Facade Pattern
definition: The Facade pattern is a structural GoF design pattern by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides that provides a unified interface to a set of interfaces in a subsystem. The facade defines a higher-level interface that makes the subsystem easier to use and reduces the many dependencies between clients and implementation classes, for example by hiding validation, authorization and billing behind one simple payment interface.

title: GoF-Factory Method Pattern
definition: The Factory Method pattern, also known as Virtual Constructor, is a creational GoF design pattern by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides that defines an interface for creating an object but lets subclasses decide which class to instantiate. It suits a class that cannot anticipate which objects it must create, and it allows new types to be added without changing existing code.

title: GoF-Flyweight Pattern
definition: The Flyweight pattern is a structural GoF design pattern by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides that uses sharing to support large numbers of fine-grained objects efficiently. Instead of holding many separate instances, the system shares common objects among their users, which reduces memory consumption when an application needs very many small objects.

title: GoF-Interpreter Pattern
definition: The Interpreter pattern is a behavioral GoF design pattern by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides that, for a given language, defines a representation of its grammar together with an interpreter that uses this representation to interpret sentences in the language. It suits small grammars and domain-specific languages, where each grammar rule becomes part of the representation the interpreter evaluates.

title: GoF-Iterator Pattern
definition: The Iterator pattern is a behavioral GoF design pattern by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides that provides a way to access the elements of an aggregate object sequentially without exposing its underlying representation. The traversal moves into a separate iterator object, which allows several traversals of the same aggregate and a uniform interface across different structures, such as depth-first and breadth-first walks of a tree.

title: GoF-Mediator Pattern
definition: The Mediator pattern is a behavioral GoF design pattern by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides that defines an object which encapsulates how a set of objects interact. The objects no longer refer to each other explicitly but communicate through the mediator, which promotes loose coupling, makes each object easier to reuse and centralizes complex coordination, for example between form, list and filter components in a UI.

title: GoF-Memento Pattern
definition: The Memento pattern is a behavioral GoF design pattern by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides that captures and externalizes an object's internal state without violating encapsulation, so that the object can be restored to this state later. Such snapshots are the basis for undo and other forms of state preservation.

title: GoF-Observer Pattern
definition: The Observer pattern, also known as Publish-Subscribe or Event-Listener, is a behavioral GoF design pattern by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides that defines a one-to-many dependency between objects. When one object changes state, all its dependents are notified and updated automatically. The subject does not need to know who its observers are or how many there are, as when a data model updates the UI through events.

title: GoF-Prototype Pattern
definition: The Prototype pattern is a creational GoF design pattern by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides that specifies the kinds of objects to create through a prototypical instance and creates new objects by copying it. Cloning a prototype keeps a system independent of how its products are created, lets the classes to instantiate be chosen at runtime and avoids a factory hierarchy that mirrors the product hierarchy.

title: GoF-Proxy Pattern
definition: The Proxy pattern is a structural GoF design pattern by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides that provides a surrogate or placeholder for another object to control access to it. The proxy offers a more versatile reference than a simple pointer and comes in remote, virtual, protection and smart reference variants, for example a caching proxy that answers repeated API requests from its cache.

title: GoF-Singleton Pattern
definition: The Singleton pattern is a creational GoF design pattern by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides that ensures a class has only one instance and provides a global point of access to it. It targets cases where exactly one instance must exist. Modern practice widely treats it as an anti-pattern because it introduces global mutable state and hides dependencies, and Erich Gamma himself said in 2009 that he favours dropping it from the catalog.

title: GoF-State Pattern
definition: The State pattern, also known as Objects for States, is a behavioral GoF design pattern by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides that lets an object alter its behavior when its internal state changes, so that the object appears to change its class. Each state encapsulates its own behavior in a separate object, which replaces large state-dependent conditional statements and offers one way to implement a finite state machine.

title: GoF-Strategy Pattern
definition: The Strategy pattern is a behavioral GoF design pattern by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides that defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each one and makes them interchangeable. The algorithm can then vary independently from the clients that use it. The pattern suits related classes that differ only in behavior, several variants of one algorithm, and algorithms whose data clients should not know about.

title: GoF-Template Method Pattern
definition: The Template Method pattern is a behavioral GoF design pattern by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides that defines the skeleton of an algorithm in an operation and defers some steps to subclasses. The invariant parts are implemented once in a common class, while subclasses supply the varying steps, as in a report generator whose sequence of loading, transforming and formatting stays fixed.

title: GoF-Visitor Pattern
definition: The Visitor pattern is a behavioral GoF design pattern by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides that represents an operation to be performed on the elements of an object structure. It lets you define a new operation without changing the classes of the elements on which it operates, because the operation lives in a separate visitor object and is selected through double dispatch.

title: GoM
definition: GoM — Grundsätze ordnungsmäßiger Modellierung, the Principles of Proper Modeling — is a set of quality principles for models, published by Jörg Becker, Michael Rosemann, and Rolf Schütte in 1995. Its six principles are correctness, relevance, economic efficiency, clarity, comparability, and systematic design. They help assess whether a model, such as a business process model, is fit for its intended purpose.

title: Goodhart’s Law
definition: Goodhart's Law is the observation by Charles Goodhart (1975), generalised by Marilyn Strathern in 1997, that when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Once a metric is tied to incentives, people optimise the metric instead of the goal it stands for, which invites gaming and surrogation. Balanced counter-metrics, measures kept for learning, and qualitative signals guard against this.

title: GOV.UK Design System
definition: The GOV.UK Design System is the UK Government Digital Service's library of styles, components and patterns for public services, launched in 2018. It is known for one question per page, a start page, a check-answers page, clear error summaries and plain English, all tested with real users.

title: GRASP
definition: GRASP — General Responsibility Assignment Software Patterns — is a set of nine principles, described by Craig Larman in “Applying UML and Patterns”, for deciding which class takes which responsibility in object-oriented design. They are Information Expert, Creator, Controller, Low Coupling, High Cohesion, Polymorphism, Pure Fabrication, Indirection, and Protected Variations. Applied together, they keep classes focused and loosely coupled.

title: GTD — Getting Things Done
definition: Getting Things Done (GTD) is David Allen's personal productivity method that moves every commitment out of the head into a trusted external system. It runs in five steps, Capture, Clarify, Organize, Reflect and Engage: items are collected in inboxes, turned into concrete next actions, sorted into lists such as Projects, Waiting For and Someday/Maybe, and checked in a Weekly Review. The two-minute rule handles small tasks at once.

title: Gutes Deutsch nach Wolf Schneider
definition: Gutes Deutsch nach Wolf Schneider is the set of German writing rules Wolf Schneider laid down in books such as Deutsch für Profis (1982): short sentences, active voice, verbs instead of nouns, concrete words, and no filler words. Every sentence serves the reader, never the writer's wish to impress. Linguists contest his claim of general validity and his polemics, while the craft rules remain largely uncontested in journalism training.

title: Hemingway Bridge
definition: The Hemingway Bridge is a session-management technique traced to Ernest Hemingway: you end each work session deliberately before a natural stopping point, while you still know exactly what comes next. You leave a bridge for re-entry, such as an unfinished sentence, a TODO comment, or a short note on the next steps. This preserves momentum across interruptions and removes the blank-page moment at the start of the next session.

title: Hero’s Journey
proponents: Joseph Campbell ("The Hero with a Thousand Faces")
definition: The Hero’s Journey, or monomyth, is a narrative pattern that Joseph Campbell described in “The Hero with a Thousand Faces” (1949) and Christopher Vogler adapted for writers in “The Writer’s Journey” (1992). A hero leaves the ordinary world at a call to adventure, crosses a threshold, survives a central ordeal, and returns transformed with something of value. It structures stories around the protagonist’s fundamental change.

title: HEXACO Personality Model
definition: HEXACO is a six-factor model of personality structure by Kibeom Lee and Michael C. Ashton. It describes personality along six continuous dimensions — Honesty-Humility, Emotionality, eXtraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, and Openness to Experience — that recurred in lexical studies across many languages. Its distinctive addition to the Big Five is Honesty-Humility, which predicts unethical, exploitative, and manipulative behaviour.

title: Hexagonal Architecture (Ports & Adapters)
definition: Hexagonal Architecture, also called Ports and Adapters, is an architectural style described by Alistair Cockburn in 2005. It places the core domain at the center, isolated from external concerns: ports are interfaces that define how the application communicates, and adapters connect them to user interfaces, APIs, databases, and message queues. Dependencies point inward, so core logic stays independent of frameworks and easy to test in isolation.

title: Hoshin Kanri
definition: Hoshin Kanri (“direction management”), also called Policy or Strategy Deployment, is a strategic planning method from Japanese manufacturing that aligns a whole organisation behind a few breakthrough objectives. Long-term True North goals become annual priorities, which a one-page X-Matrix links to improvement priorities, metrics, and owners. Catchball negotiates goals between levels, and regular PDCA reviews keep the strategy adapted to reality.

title: IEC 61508 SIL Levels
definition: IEC 61508 Safety Integrity Levels are four classes of risk reduction, SIL 1 to SIL 4, defined in the IEC standard for the functional safety of electrical, electronic, and programmable electronic safety-related systems. Hazard analysis and risk assessment determine the required level, and each level sets a band for the probability of failure on demand (PFD). The standard also sets hardware and software requirements and a safety lifecycle from concept to decommissioning.

title: Impact Mapping
definition: Impact Mapping is Gojko Adzic's collaborative planning technique, described in his 2012 book, that links what a team builds to a business goal across four levels: Goal, Actors, Impacts and Deliverables, answering Why, Who, How and What. Drawn as a mind map, it makes assumptions explicit, prevents scope creep by tying every deliverable to a goal, and serves as a goal-oriented alternative to feature roadmaps.

title: Inverted Pyramid Style
definition: The Inverted Pyramid Style is a journalistic writing convention, attributed to late-19th-century American wire-service reporting, that puts the most newsworthy facts first and supporting detail in decreasing order of importance. Readers can stop anywhere and still have the essentials, and editors can cut from the bottom. Unlike BLUF it allows a long optional tail, and unlike the Pyramid Principle it optimises for skimming rather than a complete argument.

title: INVEST
definition: INVEST is a mnemonic checklist for the quality of user stories, from Bill Wake’s “INVEST in Good Stories, and SMART Tasks” (2003). A good story is Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, and Testable. Teams use it to judge whether a story is ready for a sprint or must first be split or refined.

title: Integration Operation Segregation Principle (IOSP)
definition: The Integration Operation Segregation Principle (IOSP) is a function-design rule from the Clean Code Developer school of Ralf Westphal and Stefan Lieser: a function either contains logic or calls other functions, never both. Operations hold the logic and form the leaves of the function tree; integrations only compose other functions and form its branches. Operations thus become unit-testable without mocks, and the Single Level of Abstraction Principle follows automatically.

title: Ishikawa Diagram
definition: The Ishikawa diagram, or fishbone diagram, is a cause-and-effect diagram that Kaoru Ishikawa popularised in the 1960s at the Kawasaki shipyards, and one of the seven basic tools of quality. The effect sits at the head of the fish, and labelled bones such as the 5 Ms hold parallel causes and their sub-causes. It is structured brainstorming: it produces a list of suspects that data must then confirm or rule out.

title: ISO/IEC 25010
definition: ISO/IEC 25010 is the SQuaRE product quality model from ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 7, which replaced ISO/IEC 9126 and gives stakeholders a shared vocabulary for software quality. The 2011 edition defines eight characteristics, from Functional Suitability to Portability, each with sub-characteristics, plus a Quality in Use model with five characteristics. The current 2023 edition has nine characteristics and adds Safety, so name the edition when the difference matters.

title: Jidoka
definition: Jidoka, or autonomation, is the Toyota Production System principle of automation with a human touch: a machine or operator stops the line as soon as an abnormality appears, instead of passing defects downstream. It goes back to Sakichi Toyoda's self-stopping looms, and Taiichi Ohno made it one of the two pillars of TPS beside Just-in-Time. Every stop follows four steps: detect, stop, fix or contain, and investigate the root cause.

title: Jobs To Be Done (JTBD)
definition: Jobs To Be Done (JTBD), in Clayton Christensen’s interpretation, is a framework that explains customer choices by the progress people want to make in a particular context. Customers “hire” a product to do a job — functional, emotional, or social — and “fire” it when it falls short. Anything that solves the same job counts as competition, and unmet or poorly served jobs mark innovation opportunities.

title: Kaizen
definition: Kaizen is the Japanese management philosophy of continuous improvement, popularised in the West by Masaaki Imai: small changes made by the people doing the work, by everyone, everywhere, every day. Each gain is written into the standard, which becomes the floor for the next improvement. Kaikaku, radical change, is its deliberate contrast, and critics note that the Western week-long kaizen event often replaced the daily habit.

title: Kano Model
definition: The Kano Model is Noriaki Kano's customer satisfaction model, first published in 1984 in the Japanese journal Hinshitsu, which treats satisfaction and dissatisfaction as two separate axes. A paired functional and dysfunctional questionnaire sorts each feature into one of five categories: Must-be, One-dimensional, Attractive, Indifferent and Reverse. Categories decay over time, as today's delighter becomes tomorrow's must-be, and the model helps prioritise a backlog beyond raw business value.

title: Karpathy’s LLM Wiki
definition: Karpathy's LLM Wiki is a knowledge-base pattern Andrej Karpathy published in April 2026, in which an LLM reads each source once and compiles what it learns into a persistent set of interlinked markdown pages, instead of retrieving raw chunks for every question. It has three layers: immutable raw sources, the LLM-owned wiki, and a schema file such as CLAUDE.md. Ingest, query with filing back, and periodic lint passes keep the wiki compounding, with index.md and log.md for orientation.

title: Keep a Changelog
tags: Added Changed Deprecated Removed Fixed Security
definition: Keep a Changelog is Olivier Lacan's convention for a human-curated CHANGELOG.md file, published at keepachangelog.com and built on the principle that changelogs are for humans, not machines. Entries are grouped under six fixed change types, Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed and Security, with the latest version first, YYYY-MM-DD dates, and an Unreleased section at the top. It explicitly rejects commit-log dumps: machines can draft, but humans curate.

title: Kishōtenketsu
proponents: Traditional Chinese and Japanese narrative tradition; Tzvetan Todorov (structural analysis)
definition: Kishōtenketsu (起承転結) is a four-part narrative structure from the classical Chinese and Japanese poetic and narrative tradition. Ki introduces, Shō develops, Ten adds an unexpected element that recontextualises everything before it, and Ketsu reconciles all parts into a harmonious resolution. Unlike Western three-act structure, it needs no protagonist-antagonist conflict: tension comes from juxtaposition, not opposition.

title: KISS Principle
definition: The KISS principle, Keep It Simple, Stupid, is a design principle associated with Kelly Johnson of Lockheed Skunk Works in the 1960s and later Robert C. Martin, holding that systems work best when kept simple. It favours the simplest working solution, readability over cleverness, and no complexity beyond what the current problem requires. Simpler designs reduce the cognitive load of understanding, maintaining and extending a system, and the principle pairs with YAGNI.

title: Kotter’s 8-Step Change Model
definition: Kotter's 8-Step Change Model is a framework for leading organisational change, introduced by John P. Kotter of Harvard Business School in 1995 and expanded in his 1996 book Leading Change. It sequences eight steps — from establishing urgency and forming a guiding coalition through communicating a vision and generating short-term wins to anchoring the change in corporate culture. Each step inverts a common error of failed transformations.

title: Laddering (Interview Technique)
definition: Laddering is an interview technique, originated by George Kelly and Dennis Hinkle in Personal Construct Psychology and adapted for marketing research by Thomas J. Reynolds and Jonathan Gutman in 1988, that reconstructs means-end chains from product attributes through consequences to personal values. The interviewer probes upward with why and downward with how, mapping the respondent's value hierarchy in both directions. Unlike Five Whys, it surfaces motivations, not a single root cause.

title: LASR according to Toth/Zörner
definition: LASR, the Lightweight Approach for Software Reviews by Stefan Toth and Stefan Zörner, is a structured method for reviewing software systems that is more streamlined than ATAM but still focused on the key quality attributes. The team condenses the system's vision into a Lean Mission Statement, sets quantified evaluation criteria, identifies the most significant risks, and analyses the gaps in depth. It runs as a moderated, game-like workshop that delivers first results within hours.

title: Law of Demeter
definition: The Law of Demeter, or Principle of Least Knowledge, is a design heuristic from Ian Holland and Karl Lieberherr's Demeter Project at Northeastern University (1987): a method should only talk to its immediate friends. It may call methods on itself, its parameters, objects it creates and its direct components, but not on objects those calls return. Avoiding such train-wreck chains limits coupling and keeps an object's internal structure encapsulated.

title: Laws of UX
definition: Laws of UX is Jon Yablonski's collection of psychological principles for interface design, published as a website in 2018 and as an O'Reilly book. It names effects such as Fitts's Law, Hick's Law, Jakob's Law, Miller's Law and the Doherty Threshold, so design decisions can cite a known principle.

title: Principle of Least Privilege (Saltzer & Schroeder)
definition: The Principle of Least Privilege is one of eight design principles in Jerome H. Saltzer and Michael D. Schroeder's 1975 paper "The Protection of Information in Computer Systems": every program and every user should operate with the least set of privileges necessary to complete the job. Its first stated purpose is to limit damage from accident or error. Because the minimum is relative to the job, the grant should expire with the job.

title: Lehman’s Software Classification
definition: Lehman's Software Classification is Meir M. Lehman's taxonomy, published in 1980, that sorts software by its relationship to the real world: S-type software is fully specifiable, P-type approximates a real-world problem, and E-type becomes part of the world it changes. Because using an E-type system changes its own requirements, Lehman derived eight laws of software evolution, such as Continuing Change and Increasing Complexity. It explains why finished business software still needs ongoing investment.

title: LINDDUN
definition: LINDDUN is a privacy threat modeling framework by Kim Wuyts, Riccardo Scandariato and Wouter Joosen of KU Leuven's DistriNet Research Group, published in 2014. Its name lists seven privacy threat categories — Linkability, Identifiability, Non-repudiation, Detectability, Disclosure of information, Unawareness and Non-compliance. Teams use them to find privacy risks in systems that handle personal data, for example in the design phase.

title: LLM-Evaluations
definition: LLM Evaluations (Large Language Model Evaluations) are the methods for measuring and comparing the capabilities of language models. They combine standardized benchmark suites, quantitative metrics, automatic and human judgment, holistic frameworks such as Stanford's HELM, human-preference rankings such as Chatbot Arena, and red-teaming for safety. They also guard against benchmark contamination, which inflates apparent performance.

title: Locality of Behaviour
definition: Locality of Behaviour is a design principle named by Carson Gross in a 2020 htmx essay: the behaviour of a unit of code should be as obvious as possible by looking only at that unit of code. It weighs read-time cost over write-time cost, treats behaviour at a distance as the failure mode, and co-locates markup, handlers and styling as the remedy. It openly trades against DRY and Separation of Concerns where those scatter one feature across files.

title: Luhmann’s System Theory
definition: Luhmann's System Theory is Niklas Luhmann's sociological theory of autopoietic social systems, set out in works such as Soziale Systeme (1984), in which a system defines itself through the difference between itself and its environment. Systems are operationally closed and reproduce themselves through their own operations, and social systems consist of communication, not of people. Systems can only perturb one another through structural coupling, never instruct each other, which explains why direct control often fails.

title: MADR
definition: MADR (Markdown Architectural Decision Records) is a structured Markdown template for architecture decision records by Oliver Kopp, Olaf Zimmermann and the MADR community. More detailed than basic ADRs, it records the context and problem statement, decision drivers, considered options, the decision outcome with its justification, and the pros and cons of each option. Alternatives and trade-offs are thus documented explicitly and stored with the code.

title: Material Design 3
definition: Material Design 3 is Google's design system for Android and the web, introduced as Material You in 2021 and extended by Material 3 Expressive in 2025. It defines colour roles and dynamic colour from a source colour, design tokens, a type and shape scale, tonal elevation and standard components.

title: Meaningful Human Control (MHC)
definition: Meaningful Human Control is the principle, named by Article 36 in 2013, that humans must keep genuine, substantive control over autonomous systems making high-stakes decisions, not merely formulaic human-in-the-loop oversight. It requires situational awareness, a clear accountability chain that cannot pass to machines, positive human authorisation of critical actions, and the capability for timely intervention. Noel Sharkey's five levels grade how much autonomy a system holds in each critical function.

title: MECE Principle
definition: MECE — Mutually Exclusive, Collectively Exhaustive — is a grouping principle from Barbara Minto’s Pyramid Principle: split a topic into categories that do not overlap and together cover everything. It yields clean, gap-free, duplication-free structures for analysis, communication, and problem decomposition.

title: Programming as Theory Building (Naur)
definition: Programming as Theory Building is Peter Naur's view, set out in his 1985 essay, that programming means building a mental model: a theory of why the program works and how it fits its domain. The real program lives in the developers' minds, not in the code. When the original developers leave, the theory decays, and code alone cannot reconstruct it, so knowledge transfer and documenting the why matter as much as the code.

title: Mikado Method
definition: The Mikado Method is a technique for large refactorings in legacy or complex code, described by Ola Ellnestam and Daniel Brolund in "The Mikado Method" (2012). You attempt the goal naively, record what breaks as prerequisites in a Mikado Graph, revert to the last working state, and resolve the leaf prerequisites first. This keeps the code healthy, and every commit is a coherent, working change.

title: MISRA C
proponents: MISRA (originally the Motor Industry Software Reliability Association)
definition: MISRA C is a coding standard from MISRA, originally the Motor Industry Software Reliability Association, that defines a safe subset of C for critical systems; its first edition appeared in 1998 for vehicle software. It removes or restricts the parts of the language whose behaviour is undefined or unspecified, and it classifies every guideline as mandatory, required or advisory. Compliance means every violation is either fixed or covered by a documented deviation, not zero warnings.

title: Mobile First
definition: Mobile First is Luke Wroblewski's approach of designing for the smallest screen first and enhancing the design for larger screens afterwards. The constraints of the phone force focus on what matters; in CSS it means base styles for small screens and min-width media queries for wider ones.

title: Modular Scale
definition: A modular scale is a sequence of type sizes derived from one base size and one ratio, such as 1.25 (major third) or 1.618 (golden section). Popularised for the web by Tim Brown in 2011, it replaces hand-picked heading sizes with a consistent progression.

title: Morphological Box
definition: The Morphological Box is Fritz Zwicky's method of morphological analysis, developed at the California Institute of Technology for aerospace problems, that decomposes a complex problem into independent parameters and lists the possible variants of each in a matrix. Systematically combining variants and filtering out infeasible combinations maps the complete solution space and surfaces non-obvious designs. The resulting alternatives are then evaluated, for example with a Pugh Matrix.

title: MoSCoW
definition: MoSCoW is a prioritization method by Dai Clegg from the Dynamic Systems Development Method (DSDM). It sorts requirements into Must have, Should have, Could have and Won't have (this time), always relative to a fixed timebox. Stakeholders thus agree on scope together, and the explicit "Won't have" category curbs scope creep.

title: Muda, Mura, Muri
definition: Muda, Mura, Muri — waste, unevenness and overburden — are the "three Ms" of the Toyota Production System; muda covers Taiichi Ohno's seven wastes. The anchor names the triple, not waste alone. Following James P. Womack, the causal chain runs mura → muri → muda: unevenness created by the system itself leads to overburden, which regenerates the waste that earlier clean-ups removed.

title: Mutation Testing
definition: Mutation Testing is a technique for assessing test-suite quality, founded theoretically by Richard Lipton in 1971 and developed by Richard DeMillo and Timothy Budd, that deliberately injects small syntactic changes, called mutants, into source code. A failing test kills a mutant; mutants that survive reveal weak assertions. The mutation score, the share of killed non-equivalent mutants, asks whether tests are good enough rather than whether coverage is high enough.

title: Minimum Viable Product (MVP)
definition: A Minimum Viable Product is the smallest product that lets a team learn whether a specific hypothesis about user needs holds, a term coined by Frank Robinson in 2001 and popularised by Eric Ries in The Lean Startup (2011). Its output is validated learning, not features or revenue, and a mockup, landing page or concierge service can qualify. It opens the build-measure-learn loop that ends in a decision to pivot or persevere.

title: Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI)
advisory: Widely regarded as pseudoscience with low test-retest reliability — use for reflection and dialogue, not selection (see Criticism)
definition: The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) is a personality type instrument by Isabel Briggs Myers and Katharine Cook Briggs, built on Carl Gustav Jung's theory of psychological types and published as an instrument in 1962. Four preference dichotomies — E/I, S/N, T/F, J/P — combine into 16 types that describe preferences, not abilities.
