It is widely regarded as pseudoscience and suits reflection and dialogue, not selection.

title: Nelson Rules
definition: The Nelson Rules are eight tests for special causes in control charts, published by Lloyd S. Nelson in 1984 in the Journal of Quality Technology as an extension of the Western Electric Rules. Each rule flags a non-random pattern — such as one point beyond 3σ or nine points on one side of the mean — to separate assignable from inherent variation. More active rules mean higher sensitivity but more false alarms.

title: Neo-Brutalism
definition: Neo-Brutalism is a web and UI design style with thick black outlines, hard offset shadows without blur, flat saturated colours, blocky visible structure and heavy plain type. Unlike raw brutalist web design it keeps a grid and a clear hierarchy; it spread as a community trend.

title: Nielsen’s 10 Usability Heuristics
definition: Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics are broad rules of thumb for evaluating user interfaces, published by Jakob Nielsen and Rolf Molich in 1990 and revised by Nielsen in 1994. They cover system status, real-world match, user control, consistency, error prevention, recognition over recall, efficiency, minimalist design, error recovery and help.

title: Occam’s Razor
definition: Occam's Razor, or the Law of Parsimony, is the heuristic named after William of Ockham that, among hypotheses explaining the same observations equally well, you should prefer the one with the fewest assumptions. It works on explanations rather than solutions and guides which hypothesis to investigate first in debugging, diagnosis or architecture review. It is a prior, not a proof that the simpler answer is true, and belongs paired with evidence.

title: OKR (Objectives and Key Results)
definition: OKR (Objectives and Key Results) is a goal-setting framework that Andy Grove originated at Intel as iMBO and John Doerr introduced to Google in 1999 and popularized in "Measure What Matters" (2018). Each qualitative, inspirational Objective is paired with typically three to five measurable Key Results. OKRs are usually set quarterly, kept public for alignment, graded from 0 to 1, and decoupled from compensation.

title: OWASP ASVS (Application Security Verification Standard)
definition: The OWASP Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS) is the OWASP Foundation's catalogue of individually numbered, testable application security requirements, phrased as "Verify that…". It defines three levels — L1 as minimum baseline, L2 for applications handling sensitive data, L3 for high-assurance systems — and chapters from authentication to APIs. A review thus gets a defined scope and pass/fail results; citations must name level and version.

title: OWASP Top 10
definition: The OWASP Top 10 is the OWASP Foundation's ranked list of ten web application security risk categories, first published in 2003 and reissued in editions such as 2021 and 2025. The 2021 edition runs from A01 Broken Access Control through Injection and Insecure Design to A10 Server-Side Request Forgery. Teams use it for risk assessments, secure-coding training and security reviews, and should name the edition, because category IDs change between editions.

title: P.A.R.A. Method
definition: The P.A.R.A. Method is Tiago Forte's system for organizing notes and files, from "Building a Second Brain". It sorts every item into exactly one of four categories by how actionable it is, not by topic: Projects with a goal and deadline, Areas of ongoing responsibility, Resources of future interest, and an Archive for inactive items. It works with any note-taking or file management tool.

title: PDCA
definition: PDCA (Plan-Do-Check-Act) is a four-step improvement loop descended from Walter A. Shewhart's 1939 cycle and known as the Deming cycle; Deming himself preferred PDSA, Plan-Do-Study-Act. You plan a hypothesis and how to judge the result, test the change on a small scale, compare the result with the prediction, then standardise the change or loop back. Repeated endlessly, it is the engine under kaizen.

title: PERT
definition: PERT (Program Evaluation and Review Technique) is a probabilistic project scheduling method developed in 1958 by D.G. Malcolm, J.H. Roseboom, C.E. Clark and W. Fazar at Booz Allen Hamilton for the US Navy's Polaris programme. Each activity gets optimistic, most likely and pessimistic estimates, combined as E = (O + 4M + P) / 6. A network diagram of dependencies then reveals the critical path and confidence ranges for the completion date.

title: Plain English according to Strunk & White
definition: Plain English according to Strunk & White is the clarity-first writing style of The Elements of Style, written by William Strunk Jr. (1918) and revised by E.B. White (1959). Its rules include omitting needless words, using the active voice, preferring concrete language, writing with nouns and verbs, and placing the emphatic words at the end of a sentence. Linguists such as Geoffrey K. Pullum criticise the book for presenting style preferences as rules of English.

title: Plain Language (ISO 24495)
definition: Plain language according to ISO 24495-1:2023 is communication whose wording, structure and design are so clear that the intended readers can easily find what they need, understand what they find and use that information. The standard sets four governing principles: relevant, findable, understandable and usable.

title: Poka-Yoke
definition: Poka-Yoke (mistake-proofing) is a quality technique named and systematised by Shigeo Shingo and set out in his book Zero Quality Control. It accepts that human errors are inevitable and changes the process or artefact so that an error cannot become a defect. Prevention, which makes the mistake impossible, beats warning, which only signals it; the devices are cheap, simple and installed at the source.

title: Postel’s Law
definition: Postel's Law, or the Robustness Principle, is Jon Postel's interoperability rule from RFC 760/761 (1980) for TCP/IP: be conservative in what you send, be liberal in what you accept. Systems emit only specification-compliant output but tolerate minor deviations and ignorable fields in input, which helps long-lived protocols, APIs and schemas evolve. Critics, including RFC 9413, warn that blanket tolerance breeds ambiguity and security holes, and favour strict parsing with explicit versioning.

title: PRD
definition: A PRD (Product Requirements Document) describes what a new product or major feature must achieve before design and development begin; Marty Cagan and Roman Pichler are its key proponents. It covers the problem statement, goals and success metrics, personas and use cases, functional and non-functional requirements, scope and out-of-scope, constraints and assumptions, and open questions. Cross-functional teams thus share one reference.

title: Premortem
definition: The Premortem is Gary Klein's planning technique, first formally described in the Harvard Business Review in 2007, in which a group is told that a plan has already failed and must explain why. This prospective hindsight produces more concrete reasons than asking what could go wrong. Run before commitment, with everyone writing reasons independently and then sharing them round-robin, it surfaces quiet objections while the plan can still change.

title: Primer (GitHub Design System)
definition: Primer is GitHub's design system: the colour, spacing and typography tokens of Primer Primitives, the components of Primer React and Primer ViewComponents for Rails, Primer CSS and the Octicons icon set. It began as a CSS gem in 2012, and since 2026 it is styled with CSS Modules instead of CSS-in-JS.

title: Nonviolent Communication (Rosenberg)
definition: Nonviolent Communication (NVC) is Marshall Rosenberg's communication method: it separates concrete observations from judgment and expresses feelings, the universal human needs beneath them, and specific requests rather than demands. Applied to the problem space, it uncovers the real needs behind complaints and feature requests, which supports requirements elicitation and conflict resolution in teams.

title: Progressive Disclosure
definition: Progressive Disclosure is an interaction design technique, grounded in John M. Carroll's training-wheels research at IBM and formalised by Jakob Nielsen, that shows only the essential options first and reveals advanced features on demand. Limiting the visible options improves learnability, efficiency of use and error rate at once. Nielsen recommends at most two disclosure levels; needing a third signals that the feature set needs simplification, not another layer.

title: Property-Based Testing
definition: Property-Based Testing is a testing approach rooted in Koen Claessen and John Hughes's QuickCheck: you state invariants that should hold for all inputs and let generators create the test data automatically. When a property fails, shrinking reduces the failing case to its simplest form. The approach finds edge cases nobody thought of and complements example-based unit tests.

title: Pugh-Matrix
definition: The Pugh Matrix is a decision matrix from Stuart Pugh's "Total Design" (1991) for comparing alternatives against criteria. Criteria form the rows and alternatives the columns; one alternative serves as the reference, every other is rated better (+), same (S) or worse (−) against it per criterion, and summary rows total the scores. Teams use it to reach consensus and to iterate toward hybrid solutions.

title: Pyramid Principle according to Barbara Minto
definition: The Pyramid Principle is Barbara Minto's method for structuring communication top-down, set out in "The Minto Pyramid Principle" (1987). A single governing thought sits at the top, supported by MECE groups of arguments, and each level answers the "why?" of the level above. The conclusion comes first, and the SCQ framework (Situation, Complication, Question) sets the context.

title: QFD
definition: Quality Function Deployment (QFD) is a requirements method developed in Japan by Yoji Akao and Shigeru Mizuno that carries customer needs through a chain of matrices into technical, part and process characteristics, with priorities propagating at each step. Its best-known matrix, the House of Quality, maps customer needs to measurable technical characteristics, and its correlation roof exposes conflicts between them. The output is a ranked set of technical characteristics with numeric target values.

title: Quality Attribute Scenario
definition: A Quality Attribute Scenario, described by Len Bass, Paul Clements and Rick Kazman in Software Architecture in Practice, turns a vague quality goal into a concrete, testable statement with six parts: Source, Stimulus, Artifact, Environment, Response and Response Measure. The Response Measure is decisive, since without a figure the scenario cannot be tested. General scenarios serve as templates, while concrete ones fill in literal values for one system and make ISO/IEC 25010 characteristics operational.

title: Railway Oriented Programming
definition: Railway Oriented Programming is Scott Wlaschin's metaphor, introduced in 2013 and 2014, for composing functions that can fail: a success track and a failure track, with each step acting as a switch between them. Errors become values in a Result-style return type, combinators such as bind, map and mapError connect the steps, and the first failure short-circuits the rest. Wlaschin himself limits the style to expected failures at boundaries, not every error.

title: Red/Green TDD
definition: Red/Green TDD is Kent Beck's classical test-driven development cycle, described in Test-Driven Development: By Example (2002): write a failing test first (red), write the minimum code that makes it pass (green), then refactor with the tests as a safety net. Cycles are deliberately small, only one test fails at a time, and generalisation happens during refactoring. Simon Willison popularised the cycle as an instruction for LLM coding agents.

title: Refactoring Catalog according to Fowler
definition: The Refactoring Catalog is the set of named, behaviour-preserving code transformations in Martin Fowler's "Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code" (1999, 2nd edition 2018), maintained online at refactoring.com. Each entry — such as Extract Function or Replace Conditional with Polymorphism — has a name, a before-and-after sketch, a motivation, and numbered mechanics that keep the code working between steps. The names give developers a shared vocabulary for restructuring.

title: Refactoring UI
definition: Refactoring UI is a book by Adam Wathan and Steve Schoger with practical visual design tactics for developers. It teaches hierarchy through weight and colour instead of size alone, a predefined spacing and type scale, fewer borders, full colour palettes and shadows that convey elevation.

title: Regulated Environment
definition: A Regulated Environment is a software development context governed by regulations and standards such as FDA 21 CFR Part 11, EU GMP Annex 11, GAMP 5 and IEC 62304, where audits by an external authority are expected. It demands end-to-end traceability, formal validation and verification, immutable audit trails, formal change control, separated environments and reproducible builds. Effort and rigour scale with the risk the system poses.

title: req42 Requirements Framework
definition: req42 is Peter Hruschka and Markus Meuten's framework for pragmatic, agile requirements: a template of twelve sections that mirrors arc42, from business goals and stakeholders to quality requirements, roadmap and risks. Business goals are written in PAM form, Purpose, Advantage and Metric, and the product backlog runs top-down from epics through features to user stories. It is distributed as a free AsciiDoc template under CC BY-SA 4.0 and pairs with arc42.

title: Residuality Theory
definition: Residuality Theory is a software architecture method by Barry M. O'Reilly, rooted in complexity science. You start from a deliberately naive architecture, apply stressors — technical failures, but also business and organisational shocks — and identify the residue: what remains of the system when a stressor hits. You then redesign so failure happens in a controlled way, and use contagion analysis to expose hidden coupling.

title: Richardson Maturity Model
definition: The Richardson Maturity Model is a four-level classification of REST maturity for HTTP APIs, presented by Leonard Richardson in 2008 and named and popularised by Martin Fowler in 2010. Level 0 tunnels everything through one endpoint, Level 1 gives each resource its own URI, Level 2 uses HTTP verbs and status codes with their defined meaning, and Level 3 adds hypermedia controls. It is meant as a design target, not an assessment score.

title: Salesforce Lightning Design System (SLDS)
definition: The Salesforce Lightning Design System (SLDS) is Salesforce's open-source enterprise design system, launched in 2015: CSS with the slds- prefix and BEM naming, component blueprints and guidelines for the Salesforce platform. The term design tokens comes from its team, and SLDS 2 of 2025 replaces the tokens with CSS custom properties called styling hooks.

title: Save the Cat! (15-Beat Sheet)
proponents: Blake Snyder ("Save the Cat! The Last Book on Screenwriting You'll Ever Need")
definition: Save the Cat! is Blake Snyder’s 15-beat sheet for story structure, from his 2005 screenwriting book of the same name. It names fifteen beats, from Opening Image through Catalyst, Midpoint, and All Is Lost to Final Image, and pins each to a target page of the screenplay. Writers use it to pace a story and to audit it beat by beat for gaps.

title: Second-Order Thinking
definition: Second-Order Thinking is the decision-making habit of asking “and then what?”: following a decision past its intended first-order effect to what happens once people adapt to it. Howard Marks calls it second-level thinking, and Ray Dalio speaks of second- and third-order consequences. The technique follows one consequence into the next instead of listing more effects at the same level; the decisive effects are usually delayed and behavioural, and inaction gets the same analysis.

title: Semantic Versioning (SemVer)
definition: Semantic Versioning (SemVer) is a specification by Tom Preston-Werner for numbering software versions as MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. MAJOR changes for incompatible API changes, MINOR for backward-compatible features, and PATCH for backward-compatible bug fixes; pre-release identifiers, build metadata, and precedence rules complete the scheme. A version number thus tells consumers how a change affects them.

title: Sender-Receiver Discrepancy
definition: Sender-Receiver Discrepancy is an umbrella term for the gap between the meaning a sender intends and the meaning a receiver reconstructs, drawing on Claude Shannon and Warren Weaver, Friedemann Schulz von Thun, Stuart Hall and Herbert H. Clark. Because encoding and decoding are separate acts, meaning is reconstructed, not transmitted. The term names the phenomenon without fixing a cause; noise, the four sides of a message, active decoding positions or missing common ground then serve as diagnostic lenses.

title: Separation of Concerns
definition: Separation of Concerns is a design principle, coined by Edsger W. Dijkstra in 1974, that divides a system into distinct aspects so each can be studied, designed, and changed in isolation. It is the structural basis of modular software — high cohesion within a unit, low coupling between units — and shows up as layering, MVC, and microservice boundaries.

title: shadcn/ui
definition: shadcn/ui is a collection of React components on Tailwind CSS that a CLI copies into the project's own code instead of installing them as a dependency. Released by the developer shadcn in 2023, it pairs accessible primitives from Radix UI or Base UI with semantic CSS variables, so the components become the starting point of the team's own component library.

title: Shopify Polaris
definition: Shopify Polaris is the design system of the Shopify admin and of the apps that run inside it, published in 2017 with a style guide, content guidance, design tokens and a React component library. Since 2025 it ships as framework-independent web components with the s- prefix, and the React library is deprecated.

title: Simon’s Constructivism
definition: Simon’s Constructivism is Fritz B. Simon’s introduction to system theory and constructivism, set out in his book Einführung in Systemtheorie und Konstruktivismus. It describes systems as operationally closed — they can be perturbed, not instructed — and social systems as non-trivial, history-dependent machines; knowledge counts as viable rather than true, and the observer is part of the observed system. It is the theoretical foundation for Systemic Consulting.

title: Simplified Technical English (ASD-STE100)
proponents: ASD (AeroSpace and Defence Industries Association of Europe)
definition: Simplified Technical English (ASD-STE100) is a controlled-language specification published by the AeroSpace and Defence Industries Association of Europe and maintained by STEMG, first issued in 1986 as AECMA Simplified English. It combines 53 writing rules with a dictionary of approved words, each admitted in one sense only, and treats procedures and descriptions as different text types. It serves non-native readers, translators and machines, above all in maintenance and safety documentation.

title: Single Level of Abstraction Principle (SLAP)
definition: The Single Level of Abstraction Principle (SLAP) is a function-design rule, rooted in Kent Beck's Composed Method (1996) and formalised by Robert C. Martin in Clean Code (2008), stating that all statements in a function should sit at the same level of abstraction. Low-level details move into well-named helper functions, so the top-level function reads like a table of contents. This keeps small functions readable rather than fragmented.

title: SIPOC
proponents: Total Quality Management practice (no single originator)
definition: SIPOC is a one-page scoping table from Total Quality Management practice, with no single originator, that names the Suppliers, Inputs, Process, Outputs and Customers of a process. The Process column holds five to seven steps and is usually filled first, then outward to outputs, customers, inputs and suppliers. Its job is to draw the process boundary before improvement starts, typically in the Define phase of DMAIC; COPIS reads the same table customer-first.

title: Site Reliability Engineering
definition: Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) is the discipline, coined by Ben Treynor Sloss at Google, that treats operations as a software problem. Service level indicators and objectives measure reliability, and the error budget, the unreliability an SLO allows, is spent on feature velocity and risk. Further practices include eliminating toil, blameless postmortems, the four golden signals and automated release and capacity engineering, as laid out in the 2016 O'Reilly book by Beyer, Jones, Petoff and Murphy.

title: Socratic Method
definition: The Socratic Method is a form of cooperative inquiry, attributed to Socrates, that advances understanding through disciplined questioning rather than assertion. By probing assumptions, definitions, and consequences, it surfaces contradictions and gaps, helping participants refine their own reasoning instead of being handed the answer.

title: SOLID-Dependency Inversion Principle
definition: The Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) is the SOLID design principle, attributed to Robert C. Martin, that high-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions, and details should depend on abstractions, not the reverse. In practice dependencies are injected via interfaces. Business logic then survives a change of database or framework and can be unit-tested without running real external services.

title: SOLID-Interface Segregation Principle
definition: The Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) is the SOLID design principle, attributed to Robert C. Martin, that clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use. It prefers many specific, client-specific interfaces over one general-purpose interface. This spares classes from implementing methods they do not need and keeps changes to an interface from affecting clients that never call the changed methods.

title: SOLID-Liskov Substitution Principle
definition: The Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) is the SOLID design principle, associated with Barbara Liskov and Robert C. Martin, that subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering the correctness of the program. Derived classes must honour the contracts of their base classes. Violations show up as subclass overrides that break expected behaviour, as type checks in client code, or as hierarchies that break the is-a relationship.

title: SOLID-Open/Closed Principle
definition: The Open/Closed Principle (OCP) is the SOLID design principle, associated with Bertrand Meyer and Robert C. Martin, that software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification. New behaviour comes from adding new code, not from changing existing working code. Plugin or strategy-based extension mechanisms, such as the GoF Strategy pattern, are common ways to achieve this.

title: SOLID Principles
definition: SOLID is a set of five object-oriented design principles popularised by Robert C. Martin: Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, and Dependency Inversion. Together they steer code toward loose coupling and high cohesion, reducing rigidity and fragility as a system grows.

title: SOLID-Single Responsibility Principle
definition: The Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) is the SOLID design principle, attributed to Robert C. Martin, that a class should have only one reason to change. Each module or class is responsible for a single part of the software's functionality. Separating unrelated responsibilities into their own classes keeps a change to one feature from touching unrelated code and keeps unit-test setup simple.

title: SOTA (State-of-the-Art)
definition: SOTA (State-of-the-Art) is a term widely used in the ML and AI research community for the most current, best-performing methods in a field, as shown by recent research, benchmarks and empirical results. As a prompt it triggers research behaviour: comparing new approaches with earlier ones and backing claims with evidence. Because any SOTA claim is a timestamp, it needs an explicit date and source, ideally a live leaderboard rather than a model's memory.

title: SPC (Statistical Process Control)
definition: Statistical Process Control (SPC) is a quality method, founded by Walter A. Shewhart and disseminated by W. Edwards Deming, for the systematic statistical monitoring of running processes. Using control charts and detection rules such as the Nelson Rules, it separates inherent, predictable common cause variation from assignable special cause variation that calls for intervention. A process showing only common causes is in control, and SPC secures improvements in the Control phase of DMAIC.

title: Spike Solution
definition: A Spike Solution is a time-boxed, throwaway experiment that answers one specific technical question, a practice from Extreme Programming associated with Kent Beck. Its output is a decision, not a deliverable — a short writeup, a benchmark number, or a yes/no answer — and the code is then deleted. Teams use spikes to reduce uncertainty, for example when a story cannot be estimated.

title: SSOT (Single Source of Truth)
definition: SSOT (Single Source of Truth) is a design principle that gives each piece of data one canonical, authoritative location. All consumers reference that source, other representations are derived from it, and it is the definitive version when conflicts arise. Unlike SPOT (Single Point of Truth), which focuses on the implementation pattern, SSOT applies at the architecture and organizational level.

title: Story Circle (Dan Harmon)
definition: The Story Circle is Dan Harmon’s eight-step narrative structure, adapted from Joseph Campbell’s Monomyth. A protagonist in a comfort zone wants something, enters an unfamiliar situation, adapts, gets what they wanted, pays a price, returns, and is changed. It works at any scale — an episode, a season, a film — and requires the protagonist to transform.

title: Strangler Fig
definition: The Strangler Fig Application is Martin Fowler's pattern for replacing a legacy system incrementally instead of through a big-bang rewrite. A routing facade intercepts requests and sends each one to either the old system or its new replacement, while functionality and data move across piece by piece. Named after the vine that envelops its host tree, the new system grows around the old one until the legacy host can be decommissioned.

title: STRIDE Threat Model
definition: STRIDE is a threat modeling framework created by Loren Kohnfelder and Praerit Garg at Microsoft in 1999 and popularized by Adam Shostack. Its name lists six threat categories: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, and Elevation of Privilege. Each category pairs with typical mitigations, so teams can find and classify threats systematically during design and share a vocabulary for discussing them.

title: Swiss Style (International Typographic Style)
definition: Swiss Style, also called the International Typographic Style, is the grid-based graphic design of the Zurich and Basel schools from the 1950s. It sets a modular grid first, uses sans-serif type such as Akzidenz-Grotesk or Helvetica flush left, ragged right, balances elements asymmetrically and puts clarity before expression.

title: SWOT
definition: SWOT analysis is a strategic planning technique associated with Albert Humphrey of the Stanford Research Institute. It sorts factors into four quadrants: internal Strengths and Weaknesses, which describe the current state, and external Opportunities and Threats, which look toward the future. The TOWS variant cross-references the quadrants to derive strategies.

title: Systemic Consulting (Heidelberg School)
definition: Systemic Consulting according to the Heidelberg School is an approach to consulting, associated with Fritz B. Simon, Helm Stierlin, and Gunthard Weber, that analyses consulting as a form of communication. The consultant stays neutral and all-partial, works with circular questions and provisional hypotheses, and treats problems as emergent relational patterns rather than individual deficiencies. Because systems are operationally closed, the consultant cannot instruct change, only offer perturbations.

title: TDD, Chicago School
definition: TDD, Chicago School — also called Classicist TDD or the Detroit School — is a style of test-driven development associated with Kent Beck and Martin Fowler. It verifies the state of objects after operations, uses real objects wherever possible and mocks only external dependencies, and builds inside-out from the core domain logic. Design emerges through refactoring within the Red-Green-Refactor cycle.

title: TDD, London School
definition: TDD London School — also called mockist or outside-in TDD (Steve Freeman and Nat Pryce) — drives design from the outside in: start at the system boundary, mock collaborators to specify their interactions, and let the required interfaces emerge. It emphasises object roles and message-passing over verifying state.

title: Team Topologies
definition: Team Topologies is a model by Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais (2019) for organizing business and technology teams for fast flow. It defines four team types — stream-aligned, enabling, complicated-subsystem, and platform — and three interaction modes: collaboration, X-as-a-Service, and facilitating. Team boundaries are designed deliberately to limit cognitive load and, following Conway’s Law, to align architecture with organization structure.

title: Test Data Builder (Pryce)
definition: A Test Data Builder is the Builder pattern applied to the Arrange phase of a test, named by Nat Pryce in 2007 as an alternative to the Object Mother. Each builder starts from safe default values, offers chainable with-methods to override them, and creates the object with a build method. Tests therefore name only the values they depend on, instead of long constructor calls or one factory method per variant.

title: Test Double: Dummy (Meszaros)
definition: A Dummy is the simplest test double in Gerard Meszaros' taxonomy from xUnit Test Patterns (2007): an object passed only to fill a required parameter and never actually used in the test. It has no behaviour, and any call to it signals a fault in the test setup. Dummies satisfy constructor or method signatures whose parameters are irrelevant to the scenario under test.

title: Test Double: Fake (Meszaros)
definition: A Fake is a test double in Gerard Meszaros' taxonomy from xUnit Test Patterns (2007): a working but simplified implementation that is unsuitable for production. Unlike a Stub, which returns canned data, a Fake has real logic and actually processes inputs, only with shortcuts. Typical examples are an in-memory database or file system, which keep tests fast and predictable without external infrastructure.

title: Test Double (Meszaros)
definition: Test Double is Gerard Meszaros’s umbrella term, from xUnit Test Patterns (2007), for any object that stands in for a real dependency during a test. His taxonomy distinguishes five kinds: the Dummy fills a parameter list, the Stub returns canned responses, the Spy records calls, the Mock verifies expected interactions, and the Fake is a simplified working implementation. The precise vocabulary prevents mix-ups such as calling a stub a mock.

title: Test Double: Mock (Meszaros)
definition: A Mock is a test double in Gerard Meszaros' taxonomy from xUnit Test Patterns (2007) that is pre-programmed with expectations about which calls the system under test should make. Its built-in assertions fail the test immediately on a wrong method, wrong arguments or wrong order. Unlike a Stub it actively verifies behaviour, and unlike a Spy it enforces expectations during execution, which suits interaction-based London School TDD.

title: Test Double: Spy (Meszaros)
definition: A Spy is a test double in Gerard Meszaros' taxonomy from xUnit Test Patterns (2007): a Stub that also records how it was called, which methods, with what arguments and how many times. It returns canned responses and silently logs every interaction for later inspection. Assertions follow in the test body after the action, unlike a Mock, whose pre-programmed expectations fail immediately when violated.

title: Test Double: Stub (Meszaros)
definition: A Stub is a test double in Gerard Meszaros' taxonomy from xUnit Test Patterns (2007) that supplies predefined, canned responses to calls made during a test. It returns fixed values regardless of input and never verifies interactions, so it never fails a test. Stubs isolate the system under test from external dependencies such as databases or APIs and suit state-based Chicago School TDD.

title: Test Seam
definition: A test seam, as defined by Michael Feathers in Working Effectively with Legacy Code (2004), is a place where you can alter a program's behaviour without editing in that place. Each seam has a paired enabling point where the substitute behaviour is chosen, and Feathers distinguishes object, link and preprocessing seams. Seams let developers break hard-wired dependencies and put legacy code under test without first restructuring the production logic.

title: Testing Pyramid
definition: The Testing Pyramid is Mike Cohn’s model, from Succeeding with Agile (2009), for distributing a test suite across three layers. Many fast, isolated unit tests form the base, a moderate number of integration tests the middle, and a few end-to-end tests the top. Because lower layers are cheaper and give faster feedback, nothing should be tested through the UI that can be tested in isolation.

title: Thin Vertical Slice
definition: A Thin Vertical Slice is an agile delivery technique, associated with Alistair Cockburn and Mike Cohn, in which each increment implements one small feature end to end through every technical layer. A slice is small in scope but complete in depth and produces a user-observable change, so the system stays releasable after every slice. Unlike horizontal, layer-by-layer work, it surfaces integration problems early and often.

title: Three-Act Structure
definition: The Three-Act Structure is the classical dramatic model that divides a story into Setup, Confrontation, and Resolution, with proponents from Aristotle’s Poetics to Syd Field and Robert McKee. Act 1 (about a quarter) ends with the Inciting Incident, Act 2 (about half) escalates through the Midpoint Reversal to the All-Is-Lost moment, and Act 3 (about a quarter) brings the Climax and a new equilibrium.

title: TIMTOWTDI
tags: there is more than one way to do it
definition: TIMTOWTDI (There Is More Than One Way To Do It, also known as Tim Toady) is the design philosophy of Larry Wall's Perl programming language. It holds that problems have several equally valid solutions and that the best one depends on constraints, team and situation. It favours flexibility, expressiveness and trade-off awareness over enforced uniformity, the opposite of the Zen of Python's one obvious way to do it.

title: todo.txt-flavoured Markdown
proponents: Combines GitHub-flavoured Markdown task lists with Gina Trapani's todo.txt format
definition: todo.txt-flavoured Markdown is a task-list convention that combines GitHub-flavoured Markdown checkboxes with Gina Trapani's todo.txt format. Each task line adds todo.txt priorities such as (A), plus-prefixed project tags, at-prefixed context tags, key-value metadata such as due dates, and ISO creation and completion dates. The result stays readable as plain text, renders in Markdown viewers and can be filtered with todo.txt tools or grep.

title: Toyota Kata
definition: Toyota Kata is Mike Rother's name, from his 2009 book, for a pair of practice routines derived from observing Toyota: the Improvement Kata for the learner and the Coaching Kata for the coach. The learner sets a direction, grasps the current condition, defines the next target condition as a described process state with a date, and experiments toward it one obstacle at a time. The coach asks five questions, building scientific thinking.

title: Tracer Bullet
definition: Tracer Bullet development, from Andrew Hunt and David Thomas's The Pragmatic Programmer (1999), builds a thin, deliberately incomplete slice that touches every part of the final system on real infrastructure. It shows early whether the architecture, tech stack and service boundaries actually work together. Unlike a spike or prototype, tracer code is kept and refined, and each later tracer adjusts the aim.

title: Tufte Style
definition: Tufte Style means the information-design principles of Edward R. Tufte: maximise the data-ink ratio, remove chartjunk, keep graphical integrity, use small multiples, sparklines and direct labels instead of legends. The point is density, not emptiness: the space freed from decoration carries more information.

title: Twelve-Factor App
definition: The Twelve-Factor App is a methodology for building cloud-native and SaaS applications, published by Adam Wiggins of Heroku at 12factor.net in 2011. Its factors include one codebase with many deploys, explicitly declared dependencies, config in environment variables, backing services as attached resources, strict build-release-run separation, stateless disposable processes, dev/prod parity and logs as event streams. The aim is portable, horizontally scalable services.

title: Twin Peaks Model according to Nuseibeh
definition: The Twin Peaks model is Bashar Nuseibeh's view, from a 2001 IEEE Computer article, that requirements engineering and architectural design proceed concurrently and with equal status. As a finer-grained partial spiral, it refines requirements and architecture in alternation, with architectural decisions feeding back into the requirements. It rejects frozen requirements documents and aims for an architecture that stays stable yet adapts as requirements change.

title: Unix Philosophy
definition: The Unix Philosophy is a software design tradition, summarised by Doug McIlroy in 1978 and codified by Eric S. Raymond in 17 rules in 2003, that favours small programs which each do one thing well. Programs compose through pipes, with text streams as the universal interface, and each program's output is expected to become another program's input. Modularity, composition and quiet success keep tools simple and chainable.

title: User Story Mapping
definition: User Story Mapping is Jeff Patton’s technique, described in his 2014 book, for arranging user stories along the user’s journey. User activities and their tasks run horizontally as a narrative flow; stories are ordered vertically by value, and horizontal slices define releases, starting with a minimal end-to-end walking skeleton. Mapping together builds shared understanding and shows the big picture instead of isolated backlog items.

title: U.S. Web Design System (USWDS)
definition: The U.S. Web Design System (USWDS) is the design system of the US federal government, created by 18F and the U.S. Digital Service in 2015 and maintained by GSA's Technology Transformation Services. It provides usa- components such as the official government banner, design tokens and the Public Sans typeface, and it is the way agencies meet the website standards the 21st Century IDEA Act requires.

title: Value Stream Mapping
definition: Value Stream Mapping is a lean diagnostic method from Toyota, introduced to English-speaking readers by Mike Rother and John Shook in Learning to See (1999). For one product family, a current-state map records material and information flow plus a timeline that separates process time from waiting time. A future-state map and a value-stream plan then turn the revealed waste and low flow efficiency into scheduled improvement.

title: Vertical Slice Architecture (VSA)
definition: Vertical Slice Architecture (VSA) is Jimmy Bogard's approach to organising code by feature instead of by horizontal technical layer. Each feature forms an end-to-end slice spanning request, validation, domain logic, persistence and API, with only a thin shared layer underneath. Slices pair naturally with command/query separation, evolve independently and reduce coupling between features.

title: WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG)
definition: The WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG) is the W3C's informative catalogue of 30 UI patterns, such as Accordion, Combobox, Dialog, Disclosure, Menu Button, Listbox and Tabs. For each pattern it fixes one name, the keyboard interaction and the ARIA roles, states and properties, and nearly every pattern comes with a working example, so a prompt that names a pattern also specifies how the control behaves.

title: Walking Skeleton
definition: A Walking Skeleton, a term from Alistair Cockburn's collaboration with Ralph Hodgson, is a minimal end-to-end implementation that touches every architectural layer and the deployment pipeline before significant feature work begins. A single trivial user journey proves the structure: it builds, deploys, serves a request and logs an event. Unlike a prototype, it is production-capable code that is grown, not discarded, so integration risks surface on day one.

title: Wardley Mapping
definition: Wardley Mapping is Simon Wardley’s visual approach to strategy. A map places components on a value chain that runs down from user needs and along an evolution axis from Genesis through Custom and Product to Commodity. Reading how components move, together with climatic patterns, gameplay patterns, and doctrine, builds situational awareness and informs decisions such as build, buy, or partner.

title: WCAG 2.2 AA
definition: WCAG 2.2 AA is conformance level AA of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2, a W3C Recommendation since October 2023. It requires every Level A and AA success criterion, including 4.5:1 text contrast, visible focus, reflow, labels and error identification, and the 2.2 additions such as 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), 24 by 24 CSS pixels with its exceptions.

title: The Spectrum of Semantic Anchors
definition: The Spectrum of Semantic Anchors is the Semantic Anchors project's definition, by Ralf D. Müller, of what qualifies as a semantic anchor: a term that activates a rich, well-defined conceptual framework in an LLM's training data. A good anchor is precise, rich, consistent and attributable, and anchors range from domain-heavy, such as arc42, to interaction-heavy, such as the Socratic Method. Terms like TLDR or ELI5 fail because they lack definition depth.

title: What Would Chuck Norris Do? (WWCND)
definition: What Would Chuck Norris Do? (WWCND) is a qualified Tier 3 meme anchor, drawn from the Chuck Norris facts corpus and the books by Ian Spector and Chuck Norris, that activates a disposition rather than a methodology. It steers a model to commit to the most direct, effective solution and to refuse hedging and ceremony that buys no risk reduction. Cornelius Schumacher validated it across three models in April 2026; it helps break decision paralysis.

title: XY Problem
definition: The XY Problem is a communication anti-pattern, named by Mark Jason Dominus in 2001: someone wants to solve problem X, settles on solution Y, and asks only about Y. Because X stays hidden, helpers cannot judge whether Y solves it or whether a simpler approach exists. The remedy is to ask for the underlying goal — or, as the asker, to state X first, then Y, then the blocker.

title: YAGNI (You Aren’t Gonna Need It)
definition: YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It) is an Extreme Programming principle, coined by Ron Jeffries and spread through Kent Beck's Extreme Programming Explained (1999), that functionality should be built only when it is actually needed, not when it is foreseen. It rejects speculative generality, because unused code carries maintenance and cognitive cost. Design emerges incrementally from concrete requirements, and dead code is removed.

title: Zone of Proximal Development
definition: The Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) is Lev Vygotsky's concept of the gap between what a learner can do independently and what they can achieve with guidance from a More-Knowledgeable Other. Instruction is productive only inside this gap: above it the task is out of reach, below it nothing new is learned. Support within the zone is called scaffolding, a term introduced by Wood, Bruner and Ross in 1976, not by Vygotsky, and it fades as competence grows.
